claim: Stress-induced NA turnover in the cortex peaks at 45 minutes after stress onset and returns to baseline within 90 minutes.
source: NA turnover (as measured by the MHPG/NA ratio) peaked at 45 min and returned to baseline within 90 min after stress onset (Figure 1b).
evidence: Supported by uHPLC measurements showing MHPG/NA ratio changes over time, with statistical significance (one-way ANOVA with Tukey's post hoc tests; F(5, 24)=10.55, p<0.0001)

claim: Acute swim stress induces a robust transcriptional response 45 minutes after stress exposure in both dorsal and ventral hippocampus.
source: In line with our previous work (von Ziegler et al., 2022; Floriou-Servou et al., 2018; Roszkowski et al., 2016), acute swim stress induced a robust transcriptional response 45 min after stress exposure in both dHC and vHC (see Veh-C vs Veh-S in Figure 1d, Figure 1—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: Supported by RNA sequencing data showing differential gene expression between control and stress groups, with reference to previous publications

claim: Prazosin (α1-adrenergic receptor antagonist) only mildly impacts stress-dependent transcriptional changes in the hippocampus.
source: Prazosin only mildly impacted stress-dependent transcriptional changes in the dHC and vHC (see Veh-S vs Pra-S in Figure 1d, Figure 1—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: Supported by RNA sequencing data comparing stress responses with and without prazosin treatment

claim: Propranolol (β-adrenergic receptor antagonist) prevents many stress-induced gene expression changes in the hippocampus.
source: In contrast, propranolol had a profound impact, preventing many of the stress-induced changes in the dHC and vHC (see Veh-S vs Pro-S in Figure 1d, Figure 1—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: Supported by RNA sequencing data showing significant reduction in stress-induced gene expression changes when propranolol is administered

claim: Propranolol does not change gene expression in the absence of stress.
source: Importantly, propranolol did not change the expression level of these genes in the absence of stress.
evidence: Supported by experimental design including propranolol-only group without stress exposure, showing no baseline changes

claim: There are no significant sex differences in the stress-induced transcriptional response or propranolol effects in the hippocampus.
source: Despite clear sex differences in gene expression at baseline (data not shown), we found no significant sex differences in response to stress or propranolol between male and female mice (false discovery rate [FDR] <0.05; Figure 1g).
evidence: Supported by RNA sequencing data from both male and female mice, with statistical analysis showing no significant interactions between sex and treatment

claim: Direct activation of hippocampal β-adrenergic receptors with isoproterenol increases expression of Dio2 and Sik1.
source: Isoproterenol increased the expression of Dio2 (unpaired t-test; t(9) = 2.637, p=0.02706) and Sik1 (Welch unpaired t-test; t(3.3)=3.176, p=0.04428).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR measurements following intra-hippocampal isoproterenol infusion, with statistical significance

claim: The hippocampus receives its sole noradrenaline supply from the locus coeruleus.
source: We focus on the hippocampus, as it receives its sole NA supply from the LC (Loy et al., 1980; Robertson et al., 2013; Oleskevich et al., 1989)
evidence: Supported by citations to previous anatomical studies

claim: Systemic yohimbine administration leads to strong cFos expression in the locus coeruleus.
source: As expected, systemic administration of yohimbine (3 mg/kg, i.p.) led to a strong increase in cFos expression within the LC (Figure 2b)
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data showing increased cFos in TH-positive LC neurons

claim: Yohimbine administration increases noradrenaline turnover in the cortex.
source: As expected, systemic administration of yohimbine (3 mg/kg, i.p.) led to a strong increase in cFos expression within the LC (Figure 2b) and increased NA turnover in the cortex (Figure 2—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: Supported by uHPLC measurements of MHPG/NA ratio in cortical tissue

claim: Yohimbine administration induces anxiety-like behavior in the open field test.
source: Because NA mediates the stress-induced increase in anxiety (McCall et al., 2015; Zerbi et al., 2019), we also evaluated behavioral changes in the open field test. We had shown previously that acute stress increases anxiety in the open field test (Sturman et al., 2018; von Ziegler et al., 2022; Figure 2—figure supplement 2a), and very similarly yohimbine also suppressed locomotion and exploratory behaviors (Figure 2—figure supplement 2b).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data showing reduced locomotion and exploratory behaviors, with citations to previous work

claim: Yohimbine administration mimics a large fraction of the stress-induced transcriptional response in the hippocampus.
source: Direct comparison between stress and yohimbine revealed no significant differences (Figure 2d–e, Figure 2—figure supplement 1b), suggesting that yohimbine administration alone can mimic a large fraction of the stress-induced transcriptional response.
evidence: Supported by RNA sequencing data comparing stress and yohimbine-induced gene expression changes

claim: Chemogenetic activation of the locus coeruleus with hM3Dq and clozapine leads to strong cFos increase in tyrosine hydroxylase positive LC neurons.
source: In support of previous work (Zerbi et al., 2019; Privitera et al., 2020), injection of an ultra-low dose of the potent hM3Dq-actuator clozapine (0.03 mg/kg) led to a strong cFos increase in tyrosine hydroxylase (TH) positive LC neurons in hM3Dq+, but not in hM3Dq- animals (Figure 2g).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data with statistical analysis (one-way ANOVA; F(3, 23)=135.4, p=9.34e-15) and citations to previous work

claim: Chemogenetic LC activation leads to rapid and sustained increase in hippocampal noradrenaline in both females and males.
source: We found that chemogenetic LC activation leads to a rapid and sustained increase in hippocampal NA in both females and males (Figure 2—figure supplement 1c–e).
evidence: Supported by fiber photometry recordings using genetically encoded NA sensors

claim: Chemogenetic LC activation induces an anxiety-like phenotype in the open field test.
source: Behaviorally, chemogenetic LC activation induced an anxiety-like phenotype in the open field test, similar to the response to yohimbine (Figure 2—figure supplement 2c).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data showing reduced locomotion and exploratory behaviors

claim: Chemogenetic LC activation induces significant transcriptomic changes in the dorsal and ventral hippocampus.
source: Transcriptomic analysis revealed that chemogenetic LC activation induced significant transcriptomic changes that were similar in the dHC and vHC (Figure 2h).
evidence: Supported by RNA sequencing data comparing hM3Dq+ and hM3Dq- animals after clozapine injection

claim: Short optogenetic LC activation at 5 Hz triggers an almost instantaneous, sharp increase in hippocampal noradrenaline release in both females and males.
source: We found that short (10 s) activation with 5 Hz triggered an almost instantaneous, sharp increase in hippocampal NA release in both females and males (Figure 2—figure supplement 1g–h).
evidence: Supported by fiber photometry recordings using NA sensors during optogenetic stimulation

claim: Optogenetic LC activation at 5 Hz leads to significant cFos increase in the stimulated LC hemisphere.
source: Optogenetic LC activation led to a significant cFos increase only in the stimulated LC hemisphere of ChR2+ animals, and these changes were significant at both time points (Figure 2j).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data showing cFos expression in TH-positive neurons

claim: Optogenetic LC stimulation at 5 Hz increases cortical noradrenaline turnover at 45 and 90 minutes after stimulation onset.
source: Stimulated ChR2+ animals also showed a significant increase in the MHPG/NA ratio 45 and 90 min after stimulation onset compared to controls (Figure 2k).
evidence: Supported by uHPLC measurements of MHPG/NA ratio with statistical significance

claim: Tonic 5 Hz activation of the LC leads to immediate pupil dilation in ChR2+ but not ChR2- animals.
source: Additionally, we found that tonic 5 Hz activation of the LC led to immediate pupil dilation in ChR2+, but not in ChR2- animals (Figure 2l), as previously described (Privitera et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by pupillometry data with citation to previous work

claim: Unilateral 5 Hz optogenetic LC stimulation induces significant transcriptomic changes at 45 minutes in the ipsilateral ventral hippocampus.
source: Similar to the effects of acute stress and chemogenetic LC activation, unilateral 5 Hz stimulation of the LC induced significant transcriptomic changes at the 45 min time point in the ipsilateral vHC of ChR2+ mice compared to controls (Figure 2m).
evidence: Supported by RNA sequencing data comparing ChR2+ and ChR2- animals after optogenetic stimulation

claim: Most transcriptomic changes induced by optogenetic LC stimulation disappear 90 minutes after stimulation onset.
source: Notably, most of these changes disappeared again 90 min after stimulation onset, indicating that the LC-NA system mainly induces an early wave of transcriptomic changes in the hippocampus, which are not maintained over longer periods of time.
evidence: Supported by RNA sequencing data at 45 and 90 minute timepoints showing temporal dynamics

claim: The top 10 most LC-NA-responsive genes are Dio2, Ppp1r3c, Ppp1r3g, Sik1, Tsc22d3, Ppp1r3d, F3, Sertad1, Nr4a1, and Timp3.
source: The top 10 genes were Dio2, Ppp1r3c, Ppp1r3g, Sik1, Tsc22d3, Ppp1r3d, F3, Sertad1, Nr4a1, and Timp3.
evidence: Supported by cumulative rank analysis across multiple experiments involving stress, pharmacological, chemogenetic, and optogenetic manipulations

claim: Expression of LC-NA-responsive genes is similarly affected by tonic 3 Hz, 5 Hz and phasic 15 Hz LC stimulation.
source: Surprisingly, we found that expression of these genes was similarly affected by tonic 3 Hz, 5 Hz and phasic 15 Hz LC stimulation (Figure 3b).
evidence: Supported by RNA sequencing data comparing different optogenetic stimulation frequencies

claim: The molecular consequences of noradrenaline release are independent of the firing intensity and activity pattern of LC neurons.
source: These findings suggest that in contrast to circuit-wide changes, the molecular consequences to NA release are independent of the firing intensity and activity pattern of the LC neurons.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that different stimulation frequencies produce similar transcriptional responses

claim: 5 Hz stimulation of hippocampus-projecting LC neurons increases noradrenaline turnover in the ipsilateral dorsal hippocampus but not in the cortex.
source: Indeed, 5 Hz stimulation of LCHC neurons led to an increased MHPG/NA ratio 45 min after stimulation onset in the ipsilateral dHC but not in the cortex (Figure 3e).
evidence: Supported by uHPLC measurements with statistical significance (unpaired t-test; t(17.43)=–5.5997, p=2.911e-05)

claim: 5 Hz stimulation of hippocampus-projecting LC neurons does not affect pupil size.
source: In addition, 5 Hz stimulation of LCHC neurons did not impact pupil size, emphasizing the modular organization of the LC (Figure 3f).
evidence: Supported by pupillometry data showing no change in pupil size during LCHC stimulation

claim: Activation of hippocampus-projecting LC neurons affects expression of Dio2, Ppp1r3c, Ppp1r3g, and Nr4a1 in the ventral hippocampus.
source: Indeed, activation of hippocampus-projecting LC neurons affected most target genes, including Dio2, Ppp1r3c, and Ppp1r3g (Figure 3g–h).
evidence: Supported by RNA sequencing data from retrograde optogenetic experiments

claim: LC-NA-responsive genes (Dio2, Ppp1r3c, Ppp1r3g, Sik1, Nr4a1) are upregulated by various stressors including swim stress, novelty stress, restraint, and footshock stress.
source: We found that these genes are not only upregulated by swim stress, but also by novelty stress, restraint, and footshock stress (Figure 4b). This suggests that expression of these genes is robustly induced by a wide range of stressors.
evidence: Supported by re-analysis of published dataset (Floriou-Servou et al., 2018) comparing different stressor types

claim: Sik1 and Nr4a1 show characteristics of immediate early genes with a sharp rise and fall in expression within 90 minutes of stress onset.
source: Across 4 hours following acute swim stress exposure, we found two distinctive expression patterns among these genes. While Sik1 and Nr4a1 show the characteristics of immediate early genes with a sharp rise and fall in expression within 90 min of stress onset
evidence: Supported by time-course RNA sequencing data from von Ziegler et al., 2022

claim: Upregulation of Dio2, Ppp1r3c, and Ppp1r3g is maintained for at least 2-4 hours following stress exposure.
source: upregulation of Dio2, Ppp1r3c, and Ppp1r3g is maintained for at least 2–4 hr following stress exposure (Figure 4d), suggesting that mechanisms are in place to prolong expression beyond the initial rise in NA.
evidence: Supported by time-course RNA sequencing data showing sustained expression

claim: Stress-induced upregulation of Dio2, Ppp1r3c, and Ppp1r3g is predominantly restricted to astrocytes.
source: Re-analysis of a hippocampal single-nucleus RNA sequencing dataset after a swim stress challenge (von Ziegler et al., 2022) revealed that stress-induced upregulation of Dio2, Ppp1r3c, and Ppp1r3g seems predominantly restricted to astrocytes
evidence: Supported by single-nucleus RNA sequencing data showing cell-type specific expression

claim: Sik1 and Nr4a1 show broader expression among glial, neuronal, and vascular cells.
source: while Sik1 and Nr4a1 show a broader expression among glial, neuronal, and vascular cells.
evidence: Supported by single-nucleus RNA sequencing data showing cell-type distribution

claim: Dio2, Ppp1r3c, Ppp1r3g, and Nr4a1 are significantly upregulated in actively translated RNA in cortical astrocytes after stress exposure.
source: We found that Dio2, Ppp1r3c, Ppp1r3g, and Nr4a1 are significantly upregulated after stress exposure.
evidence: Supported by re-analysis of TRAPseq data from Murphy-Royal et al., 2020 showing ribosome-bound mRNA changes

claim: Noradrenaline release during stress exposure regulates a large and reproducible set of genes in the hippocampus via β-adrenergic receptors.
source: We reveal that NA release during stress exposure regulates a large and reproducible set of genes in the dorsal and ventral hippocampus via β-adrenergic receptors.
evidence: Supported by multiple experiments using propranolol to block β-adrenergic receptors and RNA sequencing

claim: For a subset of genes, noradrenaline release triggered by LC stimulation is sufficient to mimic the stress-induced transcriptional response.
source: For a smaller subset of these genes, we show that NA release triggered by LC stimulation is sufficient to mimic the stress-induced transcriptional response.
evidence: Supported by chemogenetic and optogenetic LC activation experiments showing similar gene expression changes as stress

claim: LC-NA effects on gene expression are observed in both sexes and independent of the pattern and frequency of LC activation.
source: We observe these effects in both sexes, and independent of the pattern and frequency of LC activation.
evidence: Supported by experiments in both males and females using different stimulation frequencies (3, 5, 15 Hz)

claim: Hippocampus-projecting LC neurons directly regulate hippocampal gene expression.
source: Using a retrograde optogenetic approach, we demonstrate that hippocampus-projecting LC neurons directly regulate hippocampal gene expression.
evidence: Supported by retrograde optogenetic experiments showing gene expression changes in hippocampus

claim: A highly selective set of astrocyte-enriched genes emerges as key targets of LC-NA activation.
source: Overall, a highly selective set of astrocyte-enriched genes emerges as key targets of LC-NA activation, most prominently several subunits of protein phosphatase 1 (Ppp1r3c, Ppp1r3d, Ppp1r3g) and type II iodothyronine deiodinase (Dio2).
evidence: Supported by cumulative analysis across multiple experiments and single-cell data showing astrocyte enrichment

claim: The transcriptomic response to LC-NA activation is shorter in duration than the response to natural stressors.
source: The response to LC-NA activation we observe in our experiments is short in duration. Following temporally precise optogenetic LC activation, gene expression changes did resolve within 90 min. This is noticeably different from an actual stress response, where gene expression evolves over a 4 hr period (von Ziegler et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by comparison of time-course data from optogenetic experiments versus natural stress exposure

claim: Glucocorticoid signaling can extend stress-induced gene expression changes over longer time periods than noradrenaline alone.
source: This supports the concept that NA can act as a rapid molecular regulator, whereas glucocorticoid signaling can extend these stress-induced changes over longer time periods (Hermans et al., 2014).
evidence: Inferred from temporal dynamics of gene expression and supported by citation to previous work on glucocorticoid timing

claim: Dexamethasone (glucocorticoid receptor agonist) upregulates Dio2, Ppp1r3c, and Ppp1r3g at 4 hours after injection.
source: Indeed, a recent study reported that activation of the glucocorticoid receptor by dexamethasone can induce strong transcriptomic changes 4 hr after injection across multiple brain regions (Gerstner et al., 2022). Analyzing their data we found that Dio2, Ppp1r3c, and Ppp1r3g were all upregulated 4 hr after dexamethasone injection.
evidence: Supported by re-analysis of published data from Gerstner et al., 2022

claim: Noradrenaline release is required to enable or enhance gene expression triggered via other mechanisms during stress.
source: This suggests that even if NA release alone is not sufficient to activate large numbers of genes, it is required to enable or enhance gene expression triggered via other mechanisms.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that blocking β-receptors prevents many stress-induced genes, while LC activation alone induces fewer genes

claim: Noradrenaline can increase neuronal excitability.
source: The notion that NA release could enhance glutamate-dependent transcriptional cascades is in line with physiological evidence that NA can increase the excitability of neurons (Bouret and Sara, 2002)
evidence: Supported by citation to previous physiological studies

claim: Systemic yohimbine administration can induce corticosterone release into the blood.
source: Finally, systemic yohimbine administration and noradrenergic activity have been shown to induce corticosterone release into the blood (Johnston et al., 1988; Leibowitz et al., 1988; Fink, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies on yohimbine effects

claim: Different LC stimulation patterns (tonic vs phasic) differentially affect brain network connectivity.
source: Interestingly, this is in contrast with our previous findings that these stimulation patterns differentially affect brain network connectivity (Grimm et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work on network-level effects

claim: Engagement of transcriptomic response via β-adrenergic receptors is common across different LC activity patterns, while network-level changes may rely more on α1-mediated effects.
source: This suggests that engagement of a transcriptomic response via β-adrenergic receptors seems common across these LC activity patterns, while changes on a network level might rely more on α1-mediated effects (Zerbi et al., 2019).
evidence: Inferred from comparison of transcriptomic and network-level data, with citation to previous work

claim: Hippocampus-projecting LC neurons do not project to the cortex.
source: Indeed, 5 Hz stimulation of LCHC neurons led to an increased MHPG/NA ratio 45 min after stimulation onset in the ipsilateral dHC but not in the cortex (Figure 3e).
evidence: Inferred from the lack of NA turnover changes in cortex during LCHC stimulation

claim: The locus coeruleus has a modular organization with distinct projection patterns.
source: In addition, 5 Hz stimulation of LCHC neurons did not impact pupil size, emphasizing the modular organization of the LC (Figure 3f).
evidence: Inferred from differential effects of whole LC vs. LCHC stimulation on pupil size

claim: Immediate early genes associated with neuronal activation (Fos, Egr1, Arc, Dusp1, Npas4) are not upregulated by LC stimulation.
source: Interestingly, immediate early genes commonly upregulated during stress and associated with neuronal activation like Fos, Egr1, Arc, Dusp1, and Npas4 (Smith et al., 1992; Benito and Barco, 2015; Fernandez-Albert et al., 2019; Tyssowski et al., 2018) are not upregulated by LC stimulation (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by RNA sequencing data showing lack of upregulation of these genes during LC stimulation, with citations to previous work on these genes

claim: Astrocytes are a direct and major cellular target of the LC-NA system.
source: Taken together, our findings further add to accumulating evidence highlighting astrocytes as a direct and major cellular target of the LC-NA system (Zenger et al., 2017; O'Donnell et al., 2015; Dienel, 2017).
evidence: Supported by current findings on astrocyte-enriched gene expression and citations to previous work

claim: Astrocytic pathways are important players for learning and memory processes in the hippocampus.
source: Within the hippocampus, astrocytic pathways are emerging as important players for learning and memory processes (Gibbs et al., 2008; Bohmbach et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies on astrocyte function in memory

claim: Noradrenaline enhances memory consolidation.
source: In fact, it is well known that NA enhances memory consolidation (Schwabe et al., 2022; McGaugh and Roozendaal, 2002)
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work on NA and memory

claim: Memory-enhancing effects of noradrenaline are mediated by astrocytic β-adrenergic receptors.
source: and recent work suggests that these effects are mediated by astrocytic β-adrenergic receptors (Gao et al., 2016; Iqbal et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by citations to recent studies on astrocytic β-adrenergic receptors and memory

claim: Dio2 is selectively expressed in astrocytes.
source: Dio2 is selectively expressed in astrocytes and encodes for the intracellular type II iodothyronine deiodinase
evidence: Based on established knowledge of Dio2 expression patterns

claim: Dio2 converts thyroxine (T4) to the bioactive thyroid hormone T3 and regulates local T3 availability in the brain.
source: Dio2 is selectively expressed in astrocytes and encodes for the intracellular type II iodothyronine deiodinase, which converts thyroxine (T4) to the bioactive thyroid hormone 3,3',5-triiodothyronine (T3) and therefore regulates the local availability of T3 in the brain (Bianco et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work on Dio2 function

claim: Enzymatic activity of DIO2 is increased by prolonged noradrenergic transmission through desipramine treatment in LC projection areas.
source: Enzymatic activity of DIO2 has further been shown to be increased by prolonged noradrenergic transmission through desipramine treatment in LC projection areas (Campos-Barros et al., 1994).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous pharmacological study

claim: The LC-NA system and its widespread projections could act as a major regulator of brain-derived T3.
source: This suggests that the LC-NA system and its widespread projections could act as a major regulator of brain-derived T3.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that LC activation increases Dio2 expression and previous work on DIO2 regulation by NA

claim: T3 signaling plays a role in hippocampal memory formation.
source: Notably, T3 signaling plays a role in hippocampal memory formation (Rivas and Naranjo, 2007; Sui et al., 2006)
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies on thyroid hormone and memory

claim: NA-induced Dio2 activity in astrocytes might mediate some effects of T3 on memory formation.
source: raising the possibility that NA-induced Dio2 activity in astrocytes might mediate some of these effects.
evidence: Speculative connection between NA-induced Dio2 expression and memory effects

claim: Three subunits of astrocytic protein phosphatase 1 (Ppp1r3d, Ppp1r3g, and Ppp1r3c) respond strongly to LC-NA activity.
source: Our molecular screening approach also revealed that three subunits of the astrocytic protein phosphatase 1 (Ppp1r3d, Ppp1r3g, and Ppp1r3c) respond strongly to LC-NA activity.
evidence: Supported by cumulative analysis across multiple LC-NA manipulation experiments

claim: All three protein phosphatase 1 subunits (Ppp1r3d, Ppp1r3g, Ppp1r3c) enhance protein phosphatase 1-mediated glycogen synthesis.
source: All three subunits enhance protein phosphatase 1-mediated glycogen synthesis.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of protein phosphatase 1 function

claim: Ppp1r3c expression is a master regulator of astrocytic glycogen synthesis and has been linked to noradrenaline activity.
source: Especially Ppp1r3c expression has been found to be a master regulator of astrocytic glycogen synthesis and has previously been linked to NA activity (Allaman et al., 2000; Petit et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work on Ppp1r3c function

claim: SIK1 responds to neuronal activity and regulates Na+/K+-ATPase activity.
source: SIK1 has been shown to respond to neuronal activity and regulate Na+/K+-ATPase activity (Jaitovich and Bertorello, 2010; Huang et al., 2012; Feldman et al., 2000; Bertorello and Zhu, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies on SIK1 function

claim: SIK1 detects low glucose availability and initiates gluconeogenesis in liver cells.
source: It was also found to detect low glucose availability and initiate gluconeogenesis in liver cells (Wang et al., 2020), a process which could also be important for noradrenergic activity in the brain.
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work on SIK1 in metabolism, with speculation about brain relevance

claim: The LC-NA system is a major regulator of brain-wide energy metabolism, stimulating astrocytic glycogen breakdown and increasing energy supply to target areas.
source: Our findings support the idea of the LC-NA system as a major regulator of brain-wide energy metabolism, stimulating astrocytic glycogen breakdown and consequently increasing energy supply to target areas (Coggan et al., 2018; Dienel, 2017).
evidence: Supported by current findings on glycogen-related genes and citations to previous work on LC and energy metabolism

claim: Nr4a1 is a widely expressed transcription factor that could trigger broader downstream changes.
source: Another interesting molecular target is the nuclear receptor subfamily 4 group A member 1 (Nr4a1), a widely expressed transcription factor that could trigger broader downstream changes.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of Nr4a1 as a transcription factor

claim: Nr4a1 activity in astrocytes reduces oxidative stress and inflammation.
source: Within astrocytes, Nr4a1 activity was found to reduce oxidative stress and inflammation (Dan et al., 2015; Popichak et al., 2018)
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies on Nr4a1 function in astrocytes

claim: Nr4a1 may regulate blood-brain barrier integrity.
source: and might further regulate blood-brain barrier integrity (Pan et al., 2021; Paillasse and de Medina, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies suggesting this function

claim: The dorsal and ventral hippocampus are involved in different circuits.
source: As the dorsal hippocampus (dHC) and ventral hippocampus (vHC) are involved in different circuits (Strange et al., 2014)
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work on hippocampal circuits

claim: The dorsal and ventral hippocampus are transcriptionally very distinct.
source: and are transcriptionally very distinct (Cembrowski et al., 2016; Floriou-Servou et al., 2018)
evidence: Supported by citations to previous transcriptomic studies

claim: Stress-induced transcriptional changes in the hippocampus peak between 45 and 90 minutes after stress exposure.
source: A recent multi-omic characterization of the acute stress response in the mouse hippocampus revealed that stress-induced transcriptional changes peak between 45 and 90 min after stress exposure, before gradually returning to baseline (von Ziegler et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous multi-omic study

claim: Acute stress exposure triggers a complex cascade of neurochemical events in the brain.
source: Exposure to an acute stressor triggers a complex cascade of neurochemical events in the brain.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of stress neurobiology

claim: Stress exposure immediately activates the locus coeruleus-noradrenaline system.
source: In the brain, stress exposure immediately activates the locus coeruleus-noradrenaline (LC-NA) system.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of stress response

claim: Broad activation of the LC and subsequent widespread NA release serves as a broadcast signal to orchestrate re-routing of computational resources during stress.
source: Although the LC is a heterogeneous structure with modular organization, it appears that in stressful situations, broad activation of the LC - and subsequent widespread NA release throughout the brain - serves as a broadcast signal to orchestrate re-routing of computational resources to meet situational demands (Likhtik and Johansen, 2019; Poe et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous theoretical and empirical work

claim: NA release from the LC triggers rapid reconfiguration of large-scale networks that shift processing capacity toward salience processing.
source: On the network level, for example, NA release from the LC is sufficient to trigger a rapid reconfiguration of large-scale networks that shift processing capacity toward salience processing (Zerbi et al., 2019; Oyarzabal et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous neuroimaging studies

claim: LC-NA system engagement of anxiety and memory circuits leads to increased avoidance behavior.
source: This involves the engagement of anxiety and memory circuits including the amygdala, hippocampus, and prefrontal cortex, which leads to an increase in avoidance behavior (McCall et al., 2015; McCall et al., 2017; Hirschberg et al., 2017; Zerbi et al., 2019)
evidence: Supported by citations to previous behavioral studies

claim: LC-NA system supports memory formation of salient events.
source: and supports memory formation of salient events (Uematsu et al., 2015; Hansen, 2017; Sara, 2015; Schwabe et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous memory studies

claim: The stress response triggers multifaceted molecular cascades that profoundly change brain function and behavior.
source: However, we know that the stress response triggers multifaceted molecular cascades that profoundly change brain function and behavior in response to stressful events (Floriou-Servou et al., 2021; Joëls and Baram, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous reviews on stress molecular biology

claim: Molecular changes during stress are mediated by neurotransmitters, neuropeptides, and hormones operating on different time scales.
source: These molecular changes are mediated by a large number of neurotransmitters, neuropeptides, and hormones, which operate on different time scales, to allow rapid activation, sustained activity, and successful termination of the stress response.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of stress mediator systems

claim: Several stress-induced genes can be blocked by β-adrenergic receptor antagonists.
source: For example, several of the genes that are induced by an acute stress challenge can be blocked by β-adrenergic receptor antagonists (Roszkowski et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study

claim: Widespread molecular changes induced by acute stress exposure are part of a healthy stress response.
source: The widespread molecular changes induced in the brain by an acute stress exposure (Stankiewicz et al., 2015; von Ziegler et al., 2022; Floriou-Servou et al., 2018; Mifsud et al., 2021) are part of a healthy stress response
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies and general knowledge of stress physiology

claim: Dysregulation of stress-induced molecular changes is often a hallmark of neuropsychiatric disorders.
source: and their dysregulation is often a hallmark of neuropsychiatric disorders (Girgenti et al., 2021; Rubin et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous clinical studies

claim: The contribution of corticosteroid signaling to stress-induced transcriptional changes has been well characterized.
source: To date, the contribution of corticosteroid signaling to stress-induced transcriptional changes has been well characterized (Mifsud et al., 2021; Gray et al., 2014; Meijer et al., 2023)
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies on glucocorticoid effects

claim: Astrocytic energy metabolism and thyroid hormone signaling are important for LC-mediated hippocampal function.
source: These results highlight the importance of astrocytic energy metabolism and thyroid hormone signaling in LC-mediated hippocampal function
evidence: Inferred from the identification of Dio2 and glycogen-related genes as key NA targets
